prompt.context: The Oklahoma Gas Company (OGC) is a medium-sized private company that has a rich history of drilling and producing natural gas wells in Oklahoma. They possess a diverse, and they believe valuable, set of land assets where more wells could be drilled. The company is well capitalized, but profits have been falling the last few years and are projected to be negative next year. One of the key drivers in the drop in profitability is the price of natural gas, which has dropped substantially, thanks in part to companies like OGC, that have perfected unconventional drilling techniques and have subsequently oversupplied the North American natural gas market. Natural gas prices are currently at a five year low. A larger competitor has approached management about acquiring OGC for $250M.
prompt.question: Management would like your help in assessing the $250M acquisition offer as well as identifying alternate strategies. What options does OGC have, and what course of action would you recommend?

clarifying_info.q: What is the present valuation of OGC?
clarifying_info.a: Present valuation is not readily available; more data on the topic will become available later in the case.

clarifying_info.q: How has natural gas demand trended?
clarifying_info.a: While demand fluctuates seasonally, annual demand has been stable over the past few years.

clarifying_info.q: Does OGC own the mineral rights to their land?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, OGC owns 100% of the mineral rights of their land.

clarifying_info.q: What is the impact of regulatory changes?
clarifying_info.a: While regulations have changed and may continue to change, they have yet to have a large impact on OGC's business.

clarifying_info.q: Has OGC drilled oil wells before?
clarifying_info.a: OGC has not drilled oil wells in the past, but would likely have the competency to do so in the future.

clarifying_info.q: Can OGC predict future gas or oil prices?
clarifying_info.a: Natural gas and oil prices are volatile and out of the control of OGC. Future prices are difficult to predict.
OGC has only operated in Oklahoma.

framework: Understand the current business: revenue drivers (gas production volume x price), cost structure, and why profitability is declining
Identify and enumerate all strategic options available to OGC
Quantify each option on a present-value basis using available data
Compare NPVs of options against the $250M acquisition offer as a baseline
Assess risks and uncertainties—especially commodity price volatility—before making a recommendation
Recommend a course of action with required next steps to reduce uncertainty

questions.prompt: What strategic options does OGC have?
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies at least 4-5 distinct options: (1) pivot to drilling oil wells (leveraging existing land/competency), (2) continue drilling natural gas wells in owned land, (3) sell some land assets, (4) acquire land and drill gas wells elsewhere, (5) acquire a smaller competitor, (6) go public, (7) accept the $250M acquisition offer, (8) negotiate the $250M offer upward. The interviewer should guide the candidate toward focusing on three main options: drilling oil wells, continuing to drill gas wells, and evaluating the acquisition offer.

questions.prompt: Calculate the present value of continuing to drill natural gas wells (Option: drill additional gas wells on existing land).
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for production and pricing data. Key insight: gas wells have a short 3-year life. Candidate should calculate revenue by year (production x price), discount at the cost of capital, subtract drilling cost, and add the existing gas well PV.

math.setup: Price = $3.00/mcf. Production: Year 0 = 40,000 mmcf, Year 1 = 30,000 mmcf, Year 2 = ~17,000 mmcf. Cost of capital = 10%. Drilling cost = $50M (paid at Year 0). Existing producing gas wells PV = $50M.
steps: Year 0 Revenue = 40,000 mmcf x $3.00/mcf = $120M. Note: mmcf x $3.00/mcf — unit reconciliation: 40,000 mmcf = 40,000,000 mcf, so revenue = $120,000,000 = $120M
Total PV of new gas wells = $70M + $81.8M + $42.1M = $193.9M ≈ $194M
Total OGC value (gas option) = $194M (new wells) + $50M (existing wells) = $244M
Sensitivity: a $0.20 increase in gas price would push new-well PV above $210M
math.answer: PV of new gas wells ≈ $194M; total OGC gas-option value ≈ $244M

questions.prompt: Calculate the present value of pivoting to drill oil wells on the South Texas oilfield OGC can acquire.
questions.guidance: If the candidate completed the gas math correctly, give them the oil data. The 10-year production horizon makes full DCF math intractable in an interview; the interviewer should note the complexity and provide the projected PV directly. Key insight: the interviewer provides the PV; the candidate should recognize the model uncertainty and probe assumptions.

math.setup: Current oil price = $120/barrel (historically high). Acquisition and drilling cost = $100M. Cost of capital = 10%. Production horizon = 10 years. Interviewer states projected PV of oilfield = $210M.
steps: Candidate recognizes 10-year DCF is too complex to compute precisely in-interview
Interviewer provides: projected PV of oilfield = $210M
Total OGC value (oil option) = $210M (oilfield) + $50M (existing gas wells) = $260M
math.answer: Interviewer-provided PV of oilfield = $210M; total OGC oil-option value ≈ $260M

questions.prompt: Compare the three options and make a preliminary recommendation.
questions.guidance: Candidate should rank options by PV: (1) Oil option: $260M total; (2) Sell for $250M; (3) Gas option: $244M total. A naive answer picks oil drilling. A strong answer immediately flags the risks that make this comparison unreliable.

steps: Option A – Drill oil wells: total value ≈ $260M
Option B – Accept $250M acquisition: certain cash exit
Option C – Continue gas wells: total value ≈ $244M
math.answer: On raw PV, oil drilling appears highest, but the margin over the acquisition offer is narrow and highly sensitive to oil price and drilling cost assumptions.

questions.prompt: The interviewer pushes back: are you confident in recommending the oil drilling option?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates immediately acknowledge: (1) OGC has no oil drilling experience and is entering a new geography (South Texas); (2) the $210M oilfield PV is a projection—projecting oil recovery over 10 years is very difficult; (3) drilling costs are highly variable and likely to run over; (4) oil price is currently historically high at $120/barrel and is volatile. The correct answer is that there is NOT enough information to give a firm recommendation. The candidate should recommend: thorough price forecasting for both oil and gas; a counter-offer or re-negotiation of the $250M bid; a competency/capability review of OGC's ability to drill oil wells; an independent second opinion on the oilfield PV projection.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors create uncertainty in the projected valuations, and what additional information would you want before finalizing a recommendation?

categories.name: Commodity Price Risk
ideas: Oil at $120/barrel is historically high; prices could fall significantly over a 10-year horizon
Natural gas prices may recover as oversupplied drillers cut back and short-lived wells deplete
Price forecasting for volatile commodities requires specialist analysis

categories.name: Operational Risk
ideas: OGC has no oil drilling experience
South Texas is a new geography outside OGC's Oklahoma footprint
Drilling costs are highly variable and prone to overruns
Acquiring and integrating a new oilfield carries execution risk

categories.name: Valuation Uncertainty
ideas: The $210M oilfield PV is a management projection; an independent valuation is needed
Gas well PVs assume stable gas prices over a 3-year horizon
The $250M acquisition offer may be negotiable upward

categories.name: Strategic Alternatives Not Fully Explored
ideas: Selling select land assets to generate cash while retaining core operations
Acquiring a smaller competitor to gain scale
Going public to access capital and improve balance sheet
Waiting for gas prices to recover before making a major strategic move

recommendation: Do not immediately accept or reject any option — the valuations are too dependent on volatile commodity prices to support a firm decision today
Initiate thorough price forecasting for both oil and natural gas with specialist support
Commission an independent second opinion on the $210M oilfield PV projection
Conduct a capability review of OGC's ability to successfully drill and operate oil wells in South Texas
Open negotiations with the acquirer to test whether the $250M offer can be increased, given OGC's land asset value
risks: Oil price decline would erode the oilfield PV significantly over a 10-year horizon
OGC may lack the operational competency to execute an out-of-state oil drilling program
Drilling cost overruns could materially reduce returns on either the gas or oil option
Natural gas prices could remain depressed for an extended period, making the gas drilling option value-destructive
next_steps: Hire commodity price forecasting advisors for oil and natural gas
Engage an independent engineering firm to validate oilfield production and PV assumptions
Assess OGC's internal competency gaps for oil drilling and estimate cost of bridging them
Submit a counter-offer to the acquirer above $250M, supported by the land asset and legacy well values
Model sensitivity of all three options to ±20% commodity price changes before finalizing a board recommendation
